definition: The probability law of a random variable X: it gives P(X ∈ A) for each set A.
The set of values with positive probability, for a discrete law.
Probability mass function: p(k) = P(X = k).
Cumulative distribution function: F(x) = P(X ≤ x).
F⁻¹(u) = min{x : F(x) ≥ u} for 0 < u < 1.
E[X^r] for an order r. The moment exists when E|X|^r < ∞.
Probability generating function: G(z) = E[z^X].
Moment generating function: M(t) = E[e^(tX)], where it is finite. It need not exist for any t ≠ 0.
Characteristic function: φ(t) = E[e^(itX)]. It exists for every law.
Probability density function: the density f of a continuous law, with P(X ∈ A) = ∫_A f(x) dx.
Independent and identically distributed: the variables are independent and have the same law.
The quantity that a run estimates, such as θ = E[g(X)] or θ = P(A).
A function of the draws that approximates the estimand, such as the sample mean.
One joint sample of all variables of a model, with the quantities computed from it.
The difference θ̂_n − θ that comes from the finite number of replicates.
An interval computed from the replicates. Its nominal coverage is the probability, as the method claims it, that the interval holds the estimand.
The probability that an interval method holds the estimand. A nominal coverage is the value the method claims.
The interval θ̂ ± 1.96 s/√n. Its coverage tends to 0.95 as n → ∞ when the variance is finite.
The score interval for a binomial proportion. It keeps its coverage better than the CLT interval near 0 and 1.
The exact binomial interval from the beta quantiles. Its coverage is at least the nominal value.
After 0 hits in n independent trials, the exact upper bound 1 − α^(1/n) for the probability. For α = 0.05 it is about 3/n.
An approximation of the variance of a smooth function of means by its linear part. The page uses it for a ratio of means.
The estimator of E[A]/E[B] by the ratio of the 2 sample means.
The difference of a quantity between 2 alternatives in the same replicate, with the same streams.
The same streams for each alternative. The differences between alternatives then usually have a smaller variance than with independent streams.
The integer that selects the key of the generator. The same seed and settings give the same run.
A named sequence of random numbers. The page derives each stream from the seed, the stream name, the replicate and the variable.
A generator whose output is a function of a key and a counter, so the page can compute any draw directly. Philox4x32-10 is one.
1,024 consecutive replicates: the unit of work that one worker computes.
A background thread of the browser. Workers compute blocks, so the page stays responsive.
A sampler that returns the quantile function at a uniform value.
A sampler that draws from a proposal law and accepts each proposal with probability p/(Mq).
The law q from which the rejection method takes its candidates.
The number M with p ≤ Mq. The acceptance probability is 1/M.
A sampler for a finite law that uses one table lookup and one uniform for each draw (Walker, Vose).
The value of a quantity from enumeration or a closed form, not from the simulation.
A sum over every point of the joint support, weighted by its probability.
The probability of the support points that an enumeration leaves out.
A claim tag: the statement follows from a theorem under the stated assumptions.
A claim tag: a computed value with a stated error source, such as round-off or neglected mass.
A claim tag: a value that one finite run showed. It is not a guarantee about the law.
A tail that decays as a power of k, so that some moments are infinite.
A tail P(X > x) = x^(−α) L(x) with a slowly varying function L.
A count variance larger than the count mean.
P(X ≥ s + t | X ≥ s) = P(X ≥ t) for all s and t. The geometric law has this property.
The factor (N − n)/(N − 1) by which draws without replacement reduce the variance.
A graph with an arrow from each name to each name that reads it.
One choice of the parameter values that a decision can make.
The quantity that a decision makes as small or as large as possible.
A limit that a quantity must meet, such as P(stockout) ≤ 0.05.
Maximum likelihood estimate: the parameter value that makes the observed data most probable.
A test that compares observed counts with expected counts through Σ (O − E)²/E.
Law of large numbers: for i.i.d. variables with E|X| < ∞, the sample mean converges to E[X] almost surely.
Central limit theorem: for i.i.d. variables with 0 < σ² < ∞, the normalised sample mean converges in law to the standard normal law.
The fraction of blocks whose own interval holds the reference value. It checks the interval method on this run.
A choice that breaks one assumption of a method on purpose, to show the effect on the result.
ζ(s, a) = Σ_{k ≥ 0} (a + k)^(−s) for s > 1. The zeta law has P(X > k) = ζ(s, k + 1)/ζ(s).
Simplified Technical English, a controlled language for technical text.
One random value of one variable.
One Bernoulli or categorical experiment, such as one throw of a die.
The variable whose law the distribution plot shows.
The method that draws each value with the reference sampler of its law. All 3 methods of this group give independent replicates.
The exact sampler that a law uses for independent sampling, such as the alias method for the categorical law.
A draw of n items one at a time without replacement, as from an urn.
A verdict of the decision report. The interval of a quantity or of a paired difference still includes the limit or 0, so the run cannot decide yet.
A test or an interval from replicates of a fitted model, with the estimate in place of the unknown parameter.
A law that keeps its form under sums of i.i.d. copies, up to location and scale. The normal law is the stable law with index 2.
For i.i.d. cycles, the long-run reward for each unit of time is E[reward of a cycle]/E[length of a cycle].
A reliability model in which a fraction of the faults are common causes that stop all redundant units at once.
The ratio of the variance of an estimate under a complex survey design to its variance under a simple random sample.
A function L with L(tx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every t > 0, such as a constant or log x.
Division of the sample space into strata with known probabilities, with a fixed number of replicates in each stratum.
One part of a stratification. Here: an interval of length 1/K of the first uniform of the stratified variable.
Pairs of replicates that use U and 1 − U for every uniform. Thus a large value and a small value fall in the same pair.
An expression C of the model with a known mean μ_C. The estimator subtracts β̂(C̄ − μ_C) from the sample mean of the quantity.
The variance of independent sampling over the variance of a variance-reduction design, for the same number of model evaluations. A ratio above 1 is a gain.
Each alternative draws from its own streams, so the alternatives are independent of each other.
A numerical integral that divides the interval where its error estimate is largest. The page uses the Gauss–Kronrod rules with 7 and 15 points.
The value x with P(X > x) = v. For a small v it keeps more precision than the quantile function at 1 − v.
The lower triangular matrix L with LLᵀ = Σ. Then μ + LZ has the covariance Σ for a vector Z of independent N(0, 1) values.
The set of vectors of k proportions that are 0 or more and have the sum 1.
The parameter ν of the chi-square law, Student's t law and the F law. For the variance of a sample of n values, ν = n − 1.
A prior law whose posterior after the data is in the same family. The beta law is the conjugate prior of a binomial success probability.
X = μ + sY: the location μ moves the law, and the scale s stretches it.

A tail that decreases at least as fast as an exponential function: P(X > x) ≤ C e^(−tx) for some t > 0. Then the MGF is finite near 0 and every moment is finite. Examples: the normal, exponential and gamma laws.
Two uniforms U₁ and U₂ give the standard normal value √(−2 log U₁) cos(2πU₂).
log(p/(1 − p)): the inverse of the CDF of the standard logistic law.
Program Evaluation and Review Technique: a method to plan projects. It gives a task duration a beta law from a minimum, a most likely and a maximum duration.
Generalised extreme value law: the law of a normalised maximum, with a shape ξ, a location μ and a scale σ. It includes the Fréchet (ξ > 0), Gumbel (ξ = 0) and reverse Weibull (ξ < 0) types.
Generalised Pareto law: the law of the excess X − u over a high threshold u, with a shape ξ and a scale σ.
A law on [0, ∞) with P(X₁ + X₂ > x) ~ 2 P(X > x) as x → ∞: a large sum comes from one large value. Regularly varying, lognormal and Weibull laws with k < 1 are subexponential.
The set of laws F whose normalised maxima (M_n − b_n)/a_n converge to one GEV law.
A property of a law G: the maximum of n independent G values has the law G again, after a change of location and scale. The GEV laws are the max-stable laws.
The largest value in a block of observations, such as the largest daily rainfall of a year.
The value z_T that the annual maximum passes with probability 1/T in each year.
T in years, for the return level z_T: the mean number of years between two exceedances of z_T, if the annual maxima are independent and have the same law.
An observation above a fixed high threshold u. Its excess is X − u.
E[X − u | X > u], the mean of the excess over the threshold u. For a GPD with ξ < 1 it is linear in u.
α in P(X > x) = x^(−α) ℓ(x) for a regularly varying tail. Moments of order r exist only for r < α.
The shape ξ of the GEV and GPD laws. For a regularly varying tail with the tail index α, ξ = 1/α.
An estimate of the extreme-value index from the k largest values. It is the mean of log(X_(n−i+1)/X_(n−k)) for i = 1 … k.
h(t) = f(t)/P(T > t): the rate of failure at the time t among the units that last to t.
The least or the greatest value of a support, such as the upper end point μ − σ/ξ of a GEV law with ξ < 0.
An observation mechanism that hides the exact value: right censoring shows only that T > C, and left censoring only that T < C.
An estimate of P(T > t) from censored times. It is the product of 1 − d_i/n_i over the event times t_i ≤ t, with d_i events among n_i units at risk.
LOD, the least concentration that a laboratory method can tell apart from 0. A value below it has left censoring.
Limit of detection: see detection limit.
Nolan's parameters (α, β, γ, δ) of a stable law: X = γZ + δ with Z standard. The density is a continuous function of all four parameters, also at α = 1.
An exact sampler of the stable laws from one uniform angle and one exponential value (1976).
The survival function P(X > x) against x on log–log axes. For large x, a regularly varying tail is close to a straight line of slope −α.
Each ordered observation against the quantile of a fitted law at its plotting position. Points near the diagonal agree with the fit.
Twice the difference of the maximised log-likelihoods of two nested models. For one extra parameter it has approximately the χ²(1) law in large samples when the smaller model is true.
The standard deviation of an estimator. Here it comes from the inverse of the observed information of the log-likelihood.
The behaviour of a subexponential law: a sum passes a high level because one value passes it, not because many values are large.
A law that draws a component j with probability w_j, then a value from the law of that component. The data do not show the component.
One of the laws of a finite mixture, with its weight and its parameters.
A mixture of a point mass at 0 and a count law, for data with more zeros than the count law gives.
The law of S = Y_1 + … + Y_N, with a Poisson number N of i.i.d. terms Y_i that are independent of N.
A recursion that computes P(S = s) of a compound Poisson sum with integer terms from the smaller values, with no enumeration of N.
The discrete law that gives each observed value its fraction of the data, or of the weights.
The law with the density that a kernel density estimate gives: the data values, each spread by a kernel. Here the kernel is normal with standard deviation h.
The scale h of the kernel of a kernel density model. A small h follows the data closely, and a large h smooths it.
The law of X conditioned on lower ≤ X ≤ upper. The values outside the interval do not occur and leave no record.
A law that one line of the model text defines by an expression. The input is a PDF, a log-PDF, an unnormalised density, a PMF, a finite table, a CDF, a quantile function, an MGF or a CF.
A function g ≥ 0 with a finite positive integral Z. The density is g/Z, and the page computes Z by quadrature.
The logarithm of a density. It avoids the overflow or underflow of the density itself far from the mode.
The condition that a law has total mass 1: ∫f = 1, Σp = 1, F(∞) = 1, M(0) = 1 or φ(0) = 1.
A check status: the page tested the condition by the method it states, on a grid or by a sum, and the condition held there. It is evidence, not a proof.
A check status: the page found a value where the condition does not hold. The page does not use a law with a failed check in a run.
A check status: the page has no test that decides the condition here, or its test did not settle.

A sampler that draws from a numerical approximation of the law, such as a tabulated CDF. The page states its approximation controls and error sources. The interval of an estimate does not include this error.
A sampler that draws from the law itself, up to floating-point round-off.
The inversion F(x) = 1/2 − (1/π) ∫_0^∞ Im[e^(−itx) φ(t)]/t dt of a CF at a point of continuity of F.
A quadrature rule that integrates a quadratic through 3 points of each cell. Its error falls as the fourth power of the cell width for a smooth integrand.
The largest difference between the empirical CDF of observations and the CDF of a law. Its p-value is asymptotic and assumes a continuous law.
Resampling from the empirical law of the data to estimate the variability of a statistic. Group 10 states its conditions.
A sequence of random states in which the law of the next state depends only on the present state, not on the earlier states.
The matrix P of a finite Markov chain: P_ij is the probability of a step from state i to state j. Each row adds to 1.
A law π of the states with π P = π: if the chain starts with the law π, it has the law π at each later time.
A set of states that communicate with each other and that a path cannot leave after it enters.
A state i with P_ii = 1: a path that enters it stays there for all later times.
An irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space: its law converges to the unique stationary law from each start, and its time averages converge to the stationary averages.
A Markov chain with states that do not all communicate. With two or more closed classes, its long-run behaviour depends on the start.
The average of a function of the state along one path, such as the fraction of time in state j.
The average over many independent paths at one fixed time, such as P(X_n = j).
The first number of steps n after which the TV distance between the law of X_n and the stationary law is at most 1/4, for the worst start.
Total variation distance: the largest difference of the probabilities that two laws give to one event; for discrete laws, half the sum of |p_j − q_j|.
A branching process in discrete generations: each individual has an independent random number of offspring with one fixed law.
The law of the number of offspring of one individual in a branching process.
The probability that a branching process reaches 0. For one ancestor it is the smallest root of f(s) = s in [0, 1], with f the PGF of the offspring law.
The mean number of new cases that one case causes, the mean m of the offspring law in a branching model of an epidemic.
Large differences between cases in the number of new cases: most cases cause few or none, and a few cause many. A small dispersion k of a negative binomial law models it.
The parameter k of a negative binomial law with mean m: the variance is m + m²/k, and k → ∞ gives the Poisson law.
Variance gamma: a Lévy process that is a Brownian motion with drift run on a gamma-process clock.
A process that starts at 0 with stationary and independent increments and paths that are continuous from the right.
A Lévy process with gamma-distributed increments; it only increases, and it has infinitely many small jumps.
E[(X − μ)⁴]/σ⁴. It is 3 for a normal law; a larger value shows heavier tails. The excess kurtosis is the kurtosis minus 3.
The fraction of the exposure that a lender loses when the borrower defaults.
An agreement to buy or sell an amount at a fixed rate on a future date.
A rule that closes a position when its value falls below a fixed level.
A joint law on [0, 1]^d whose margins are all uniform. It describes the dependence of a random vector without its margins.

Every joint CDF F with margins F_i can be written F(x) = C(F_1(x_1), …, F_d(x_d)) with a copula C. C is unique when the margins are continuous. Conversely, X_i = F_i⁻¹(U_i) with U from C has the margins F_i.
The limit λ_U = lim P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q) as q → 1, and λ_L = lim P(U_2 ≤ q | U_1 ≤ q) as q → 0. A positive value means that extremes come together.
The probability P(U_1 > q, U_2 > q) that both components exceed the level q. Divided by 1 − q, it gives P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q).
The probability that each component of a random vector falls in a given interval. For a copula it follows from the CDF at the corners of the box by inclusion and exclusion.
The probability of concordance minus the probability of discordance of two independent copies of a pair. It depends only on the copula.
The correlation of the ranks F_1(X_1) and F_2(X_2), equal to 12 E[U_1 U_2] − 3 for the copula pair.
The copula of an elliptical law, such as the multivariate normal or t law. The Gaussian and t copulas are elliptical.
A copula C(u) = ψ(ψ⁻¹(u_1) + … + ψ⁻¹(u_d)) with a generator ψ. Clayton, Gumbel and Frank copulas are Archimedean.
The decreasing function ψ with ψ(0) = 1 and ψ(∞) = 0 that defines an Archimedean copula. It must be d-monotone for dimension d.
A function ψ with (−1)^k ψ^(k) ≥ 0 for k ≤ d − 2, and with (−1)^(d−2) ψ^(d−2) non-increasing and convex. An Archimedean generator gives a copula in dimension d if and only if it is d-monotone.
A positive random variable V shared by all components. In the Marshall–Olkin algorithm the generator ψ is the Laplace transform of V.
The sampler U_i = ψ(E_i/V) of an Archimedean copula, with a frailty V whose Laplace transform is ψ and independent standard exponentials E_i. It is exact.
A sampler that draws U_1 and then each next component from its conditional law given the earlier ones, by the inverse transform.
The copula of U_1 = U_2 = … = U_d, the upper Fréchet–Hoeffding bound min(u_1, …, u_d).
The copula of U_2 = 1 − U_1 in two dimensions, the lower Fréchet–Hoeffding bound max(u_1 + u_2 − 1, 0).
D_1(x) = (1/x) ∫_0^x t/(e^t − 1) dt. It gives Kendall's tau of the Frank copula.
A copula with C(u_1^t, …, u_d^t) = C(u_1, …, u_d)^t for all t > 0. It is the copula of the limit law of componentwise maxima.
The limit λ_U = lim P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q) as q → 1 (upper), or λ_L as q → 0 (lower). λ > 0 means that joint extremes stay likely.
The values of one draw of a process at the grid times: a function of time, not one number.
A process whose time averages converge to the averages under its stationary law, for almost every path.
The first time at which a path reaches a given level. On a grid, the page sees only the grid times.
The difference between a quantity of the path at the grid times and the same quantity of the path in continuous time, such as its maximum.
The difference between the mean of a quantity of a time-discretised path and the mean for the exact process. More samples do not reduce it; a finer grid does.
The time discretisation X_{k+1} = X_k + a(X_k)h + b(X_k)ΔW_k of a stochastic differential equation, with the coefficients frozen on each step.
The rate r with E|X̂_T − X_T| ≤ c h^r: the error of each path. The Euler–Maruyama scheme has strong order 1/2.
The rate r with |E f(X̂_T) − E f(X_T)| ≤ c h^r: the error of a mean. The Euler–Maruyama scheme has weak order 1 for a smooth f.
Multilevel Monte Carlo: a sum of corrections between grids of increasing fineness, each estimated with its own sample size.
Stochastic differential equation: dX_t = a(X_t) dt + b(X_t) dW_t, with W a Brownian motion.
A model that draws a parent variable first and then a child variable whose law has parameters that read the parent value.
A conditional model with several levels, such as an uncertain rate, then a count given the rate.
Var Y = E[Var(Y | X)] + Var(E[Y | X]), when E Y² is finite. The second term is the variance that the parent adds.
Sampling of a conditional model in its order: each variable is drawn after the variables that its parameters read.
The fraction of a population that has a condition at a given time.
The probability that a test is positive for a person with the condition.
The probability that a test is negative for a person without the condition.
The probability that a person with a positive test has the condition.
A process with continuous paths and independent, stationary, normal increments: W_t − W_s ~ N(0, t − s).
Geometric Brownian motion: S_t = S_0 exp((μ − σ²/2)t + σW_t), a positive process with lognormal values.
Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process: dX_t = κ(θ − X_t) dt + σ dW_t, a Gaussian process that reverts to θ.
The first time at which a path reaches a given level.
For a Brownian motion without drift from 0, P(max over [0, t] of W ≥ b) = 2 P(W_t ≥ b) for b ≥ 0.
The property that time averages of one path converge to the ensemble averages of the stationary law.
The tendency of a process to move back to a long-run level, with a speed that grows with the distance to it.
The closed form of E[max(S_T − K, 0)] for a GBM: S_0 e^{μT} Φ(d_1) − K Φ(d_2).
A price model in which the price is a Brownian motion with drift, so it can become negative.
An interest-rate model in which the short rate is an OU process.
For one day, max(18 °C − the daily mean temperature, 0); the sum over a period measures the demand for heating.
The price of power minus the cost of the gas to make it, for each MWh.
A demand by a lender for more collateral when the value of a pledged position falls to a set level.
The loan divided by the value of the collateral.
A counting process with independent increments, in which the count in an interval has a Poisson law with mean equal to the integral of the rate over the interval.
The rate λ(t) of a point process: the probability of an event in [t, t + h] is λ(t)h + o(h), given the past.
Λ(t), the integral of the rate from 0 to t. For a Poisson process it is the mean count E N(t).
A rejection method for point processes. It draws candidate events at a rate λ̄ that is not below the intensity, and keeps each candidate with probability λ(t)/λ̄.
A process that adds i.i.d. jumps at the event times of a Poisson process. It is a Lévy process with finitely many jumps in a finite time.
The surplus model of an insurer: R_t = u + c t − S_t, with initial capital u, premium rate c and compound Poisson claims S_t.
θ = c/(λ E Y) − 1, the relative amount by which the premium rate c is above the mean claim rate. Ruin in infinite time is certain if θ ≤ 0.
The probability that the surplus of an insurer falls below 0. In finite time it is ψ(u, T); in infinite time it is ψ(u).
A reinsurance treaty in which the insurer keeps a fixed fraction q of each claim and of the premium, and cedes the rest.
A self-exciting point process: each event raises the intensity, here by α, and the rise decays at the rate β.
A point process in which each event raises the probability of further events for some time, so the events come in clusters.
n = α/β for a Hawkes process with an exponential kernel: the mean number of direct children of an event. A stationary version exists only if n < 1.
A Hawkes process seen as immigrants at the rate μ, in which each event has a Poisson(n) number of children after random delays.
The variance of a count divided by its mean. It is 1 for a Poisson count and above 1 for a clustered count.
A simulation of a process on a time grid, with the rates or coefficients frozen at the start of each step. Its error goes to 0 as the step goes to 0.
Epidemic-type aftershock sequence: a self-exciting model of earthquakes, in which each event triggers aftershocks with a power-law (Omori) decay and a magnitude-dependent productivity.
A Poisson process with a random rate. Its counts have a variance above the mean.
Susceptible–infected–removed: an epidemic model with a finite population, in which the spread slows as the susceptible part falls.
